bio.en: Yuriy Timen is a growth advisor who spent eight and a half years at Grammarly building its growth and marketing function into the household-name brand it is today; he now advises 4-5 subscription and consumerized B2B companies at a time (including Canva, Airtable, Otter, Hims, and Flow Health) on finding and scaling their core growth engines.
bio.zh: Yuriy Timen 是一位增长顾问。他在 Grammarly 待了八年半，把公司的增长和营销体系打造成了今天这个人尽皆知的品牌；如今他一次同时辅导 4 到 5 家订阅型和“消费化”的 B2B 公司（包括 Canva、Airtable、Otter、Hims、Flow Health 等），帮它们找到并放大核心增长引擎。

summary.en: Yuriy lays out a practical framework for how subscription and consumer companies should think about their three core growth engines-virality/referrals, SEO, and paid-and how to tell which one fits. He argues most companies are powered by a single 80/20 growth engine and warns against diversifying too early (when small) or too late (when over-reliant at scale). On paid, he explains why the current budget contraction actually creates an edge for disciplined, well-instrumented companies, and why SEO is becoming more attractive as the 'grow-at-all-costs' urgency fades. He also shares concrete benchmarks (e.g., 20-35% visitor-to-free-user and 5%+ free-to-paid conversion) and why onboarding is almost always the highest-leverage investment.
summary.zh: Yuriy 给出了一个非常落地的框架，讲订阅型和消费级公司该怎么思考三大核心增长引擎——病毒/推荐、SEO 和付费——以及如何判断哪个适合自己。他认为大多数公司其实只靠一个 80/20 的增长引擎驱动，并警告说：太小的时候多元化太早、太大的时候又过度依赖单一渠道而多元化太晚，都是坑。关于付费，他解释了为什么当下预算收缩反而给有纪律、埋点完善的公司创造了优势，以及为什么随着“不惜一切代价增长”的紧迫感消退，SEO 正变得更有吸引力。他还分享了关键基准（比如访客到免费用户 20%–35% 的转化、免费到付费 5% 以上），以及为什么上手流程几乎永远是高杠杆的投入。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: The only thing that's worse than a channel or a tactic that you tried not working. The only thing that's worse now is when you didn't give it the appropriate shot, right? And you prematurely were erroneously concluded that it doesn't work and it's remarkable how often you find that to be the case when I talk to companies, "Oh, YouTube, we tried it. It doesn't work." I'm like, "Okay, can I see what you've tried?" And then you look at it and you're like, "Oh, this thing was not designed to even have a shot at working from the get go."
turns.zh: 比“试了一个渠道或打法却没效果”更糟的，只有一种情况：你根本没给它应有的机会，就过早地、错误地断定它行不通。我跟公司聊的时候，经常发现这种事——“哦，YouTube 我们试过了，没用。”我就说：“好啊，让我看看你们到底试了什么？”然后一看就会发现：“哦，这玩意儿从一开始就没被设计成有机会跑通的样子。”

turns.zh: 我觉得八年半已经够长了。嗯，不确定我想往上取整。我知道，不过我当然是在开玩笑。对，大致就是这样。Grammarly 那是一段很疯狂的旅程，而从那一步退下来之后，做顾问这件事自己有了自己的生命力。

Flow Health, the world's most downloaded period tracker.

turns.zh: 你这增长没做好啊。

turns.en: First of all, just being mentioned the same breath as those two is an accolade in and of itself. I mean, I look up to both of them. They've gone first. Also, I credit a lot of my getting started to both of them because they've been very generous with their time when I was just kind of considering advising, especially Casey, if they listen to this. Huge shine out to both of them, but Casey especially. He's such immense when it comes to just being generous with his time. So no, there is no competition, but had there been one, I suspect I'd be in lead right now because I've done it. I've done it in a shorter period of time. I'm much newer to advising than both of those, but no, I have a ton of aberration respect both of them. They're phenomenal what they do and I learned a ton from them.
turns.zh: 首先，能跟那两位在同一个语境里被提到，本身就是一种荣誉。我是说，我很敬仰他们俩。他们是先行者。而且我起步能那么快，很大程度要归功于他们俩，因为在我还在犹豫要不要做顾问的时候，他们非常慷慨地给了我时间，特别是 Casey，如果他们听到这期的话。向他们两位，尤其是 Casey，大声致敬。他在慷慨给时间这件事上简直太大方了。所以不，没有竞争，但假如有过竞争的话，我猜现在领先的是我，因为我在更短的时间里做成了。我比他们俩都新入行，但我对他们俩是满满的、毫不掩饰的尊重。他们做的事太厉害了，我从他们身上学了很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that acceleration is fastest. Wow, sweet. So we're going to talk a lot about consumer growth strategies and your experience working with companies and a bunch of insights on things you've learned from working with companies. Before we get there just one quick question in your advising. I'm curious how many companies do you work with at once normally?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种加速最快的说法。哇，不错。那我们会聊很多关于消费级增长策略、你跟公司合作的经验，以及你从这些合作里学到的各种洞察。在那之前，就一个快速问题，关于你的顾问工作。我好奇你通常同时跟多少家公司合作？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah, so I play around with different quantities. So a couple of things. So you mentioned, you alluded to earlier that I advise full time. What I'll say is that mostly the only thing that I do right now professionally is advising, but it's not quite full time. I hard count my week at about three to three and a half days a week worth of work, which is a personal choice. And so that is a hard constraint that I'm working with. And within that constraint, I also feel like for me to do my best work and the work that I also enjoy the most and find the most fulfilling four to five companies is probably the max. If I try to go beyond that, the overhead that it creates in terms of the cost of context switching just becomes overwhelming. I feel like I'm not showing up as best as I can with each individual company.
turns.zh: 好，我会在不同数量之间调整。你说我全职做顾问，我前面也提到过。我想说的是，现在我在职业上做的唯一一件事基本就是做顾问，但又不完全是全职。我严格把一周的工作时间控制在大概三到三天半，这是我个人的选择。所以这是我工作时的一个硬约束。在这个约束之内，我也觉得，要让我做出最好的、也是我最享受、最有成就感的工作，四到五家公司大概就是上限了。如果我试图超过这个数，频繁切换上下文带来的额外开销就会变得难以承受。我会觉得我对每家公司都没能拿出最好的状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As early plug or anti plug, depending on how you answer this. Are you looking for more companies to work with right now or are you just like, "Don't even try. I am so at capacity right now."?
turns.zh: 作为一个提前的推荐，或者反推荐，取决于你怎么回答。你现在还想接更多公司合作吗？还是说你就像“别试了，我现在已经满到极限了”？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I'm so at capacity right now. I've also just been very fortunate to always be at capacity. But I think for every four to five companies that I'm working with, think of it as a concentric circles, right? There are another, maybe 10 to a dozen companies that we're actively exploring if we want to work together in the future. And then there is another concentric circle so maybe 30 plus companies that I'm just friends with. So I'll take the plug. I'm always up for meeting Austin founders working on important problems.
turns.zh: 我现在真的已经满到极限了。而且我很幸运，一直以来都是满的。但我觉得，每四到五家我正在合作的公司，可以想成一个同心圆，对吧？外面还有大概十到十二家公司，我们在积极探索将来要不要一起合作。再外面还有一个同心圆，大概三十多家公司，只是我朋友。所以我会接受这个推荐。我随时乐意认识在做重要问题的创始人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Well, we're in the plug I guess. How do people find you online? What's your Twitter?
turns.zh: 酷。那我们算是在做推荐了。大家怎么在网上找到你？你的 Twitter 是什么？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I mean, honestly, probably throw Lenny's podcast. That's one, but honestly LinkedIn is really the only place I'm pretty low key otherwise.
turns.zh: 说实话，可能就是靠 Lenny 的播客吧，这是一个渠道。但要说别的，我其实挺低调的，LinkedIn 差不多是我唯一在用的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. That was a lot of Meta stuff. So let's get into some meat stuff here. So you talked to a lot of consumer startups. You help them figure out how to grow, how to evolve their product, something I'm always curious about and I love your thoughts on is when you look at a consumer startup, I imagine there's a few archetypes of how they grow. I'm curious if that's a mental model you use when you're like, "Oh, I see company X. They're probably going to grow this way, and here's what they should focus on." How do you see that?
turns.zh: 好，太棒了。刚才聊了很多元层面的东西。那我们进入点实在的内容。你跟很多消费级创业公司聊过，你帮他们想怎么增长、怎么演化产品，这点我一直很好奇，也很想听你的想法：当你看一家消费级创业公司时，我猜有几种典型增长模型。我好奇这是不是你脑子里的一个思维模型——“哦，我看到 X 公司，他们大概会这样增长，他们应该聚焦在哪儿。”你是怎么看的？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Great question. I think there are ways to answer that. My sweet spot is subscription properties and it's not just consumer. I do work with a lot of B2B companies. It's just that most of them, but what they all have in common is they lean into consumerized type of growth loops and growth motions. So they're very kind of self-serve nature or have meaningful self-serve engines. So if I think about subscription companies, I think there are probably a couple of buckets that I see them falling into. If you were able to nail your unit economics and you have really strong consumer LTVs, think Grammarly, think Canva. The single player LTVs for those companies are very, very high. They're kind of average S&B LTVs for B2B companies.
turns.zh: 好问题。我觉得可以从几个角度来回答。我最擅长的是订阅型产品，而且不只是消费级。我也跟很多 B2B 公司合作。只是大多数——它们共同的一点，是都倚重那种“消费化”的增长闭环和增长打法。所以它们很有自助服务的性质，或者有很扎实的自助服务引擎。所以说到订阅公司，我觉得大概能分成几类。如果你能把单位经济模型跑通，而且有非常强的消费级用户终身价值（LTV），想想 Grammarly，想想 Canva。这些公司的单人 LTV 非常高，差不多能达到 B2B 公司的平均水平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a number there just for folks to have a little context?
turns.zh: 给个大概的数字让大家有点概念？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I'm not a liberty to speak to those, but we're talking in the hundreds of dollars. Most consumer subscription companies that are $5 to $7 a month. Their LTVs typically cap out at 50 to 60 bucks.
turns.zh: 我不方便透露具体数字，但我们说的是几百美元这个量级。大多数每月 5 到 7 美元的消费者订阅公司，它们的 LTV 通常封顶在 50 到 60 美元。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 酷。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: And so if you have really healthy LTVs, and that usually means that you're attracting a proconsumer buyer, so they may be single player, but they're using it for work. And so maybe they're dispensing it or just the perceived value so much higher that they're willing to bear that $120 and $130 a year subscription. If I'm seeing things like that and I'm seeing that you're converting seven, like five plus percent of your free users to a paid subscriber, then there is a big opportunity to play paid and lean into paid growth loops and paid acquisition loops. There is another archetype, which is if there are network effects for instance, you don't find that as much with single player consumer subscription companies, but obviously social media, consumer companies.
turns.zh: 所以如果你有很健康的 LTV，这通常意味着你吸引到的是“专业消费者”买家，所以他们可能是一个人用，但是为了工作。所以他们愿意为每年 120、130 美元的订阅买单，因为感知价值高太多了。如果我看到这样的情况，而且看到你把免费用户转化为付费订阅者的比例能到 5% 以上，那就有一个很大的机会去投付费，去倚重付费增长闭环和付费获客闭环。还有另一种典型类型，就是如果有网络效应——单一玩家的消费级订阅公司里不太常见，但社交媒体、消费级公司显然就有。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: There may be a strong referral viral loop angle if the utility increases, the utility of the product increases, the more users are using it. Another archetype I see are companies that can lead into SEO very heavily, especially if there is a long tail programmatic angle. Take Canva for instance, their biggest initial growth loop and I think this is public knowledge was their long tail SEO strategy where any kind of design project that you could think of would search for designing. It's kind of two categories of keywords, make keywords and template keywords. So if you're searching for a template of any kind, a wedding invitation, yada yada, they had incredibly strong SEO and they were just capitalizing on all the long tail traffic. Not every product is going to lend itself to that, but I always look for that early on, because you can build incredible mold with that kind of strategy.
turns.zh: 如果产品的效用会随着使用的人越多而提升，那就可能有很强的推荐/病毒式闭环的角度。我看到的另一种典型类型，是能重度倚靠 SEO 的公司，尤其是有长尾、程序化角度的那种。拿 Canva 举例，他们最早、也是我认为公开的一个增长闭环，就是长尾 SEO 策略：任何你能想到的设计项目，大家都会搜。大概两类关键词，“做（make）”类关键词和“模板（template）”类关键词。所以如果你搜任何一种模板，比如说婚礼请柬之类的，他们就有极强的 SEO，把长尾流量全都吃进来了。不是每个产品都适合这么做，但我总会很早去找这个可能性，因为这种策略能建立起非常深的护城河。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. There's kind of like these three engines that you can tap into. I imagine the preference would be word of mouth reality and then if that isn't going to work SEO, and if that is going to work paid, maybe just to simplify it for listeners, what are kind of signals you can go after virality and invest in that and think that could work because every founder would be like, "Yes, virality. That's how I'm going to grow." Yeah.
turns.zh: 有道理。大概就是这三大引擎你可以去撬动。我猜优先顺序会是口碑/病毒传播，如果不行就 SEO，再不行就付费，为了听众多简单化一点，就是有哪些信号说明你可以去投病毒传播、觉得能成？因为每个创始人都会说“对，病毒传播，我就要靠这个增长”。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah. Honestly, the first thing you look for is that, is there inherent product network effects? It's something that it's either there, or isn't from inception from my experience. I think it's very difficult to manufacture. You'd only study when... It's very hard to manufacture product network effects if they aren't there from the get go. So Airbnb from your days, obviously marketplace very strong product network effect dynamics. You think of collaboration tools, Airtable, monday.com, Whimsical, whom we both know very strong inherent product network effects, contrast that with a company like Grammarly. It just wasn't there. It's not an inherently multiplayer task constructed communication. And so you can try to engineer that, but from my experience, it is an uphill battle. So if you have inherent product network effects, that's when I think layering on referral loops and viral loops. You think about what Dropbox has done around file sharing. That's an iconic example.
turns.zh: 对。说实话，你第一件要看的，就是有没有内在的产品网络效应。根据我的经验，这个东西要么从一开始就有，要么就没有。很难去制造。你只有在……如果一开始没有，几乎不可能硬造出产品网络效应。所以 Airbnb，你当年在那儿，显然是 marketplace，很强的产品网络效应。协作工具，Airtable、monday.com、Whimsical，我们俩都认识的，也有很强的内在产品网络效应。对比一下 Grammarly，它就没有。它本来就不是多人协作或沟通的任务。所以你可以试着去设计，但根据我的经验，那是一场艰苦的逆水行舟。所以如果你有内在的产品网络效应，那就是我说的该叠加推荐闭环和病毒闭环的时候。想想 Dropbox 在文件分享上做的事，那是经典案例。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Then it's really powerful. I think that there is another case where referral and viral loops could work even when there are inherent network effects. If you have a really beloved product, beloved brand. There's a company out of Australia that I have opportunity to invest it called Laika. They do fresh dog food subscriptions and incredibly beloved brand, a premium product. And so they're able to lean into a give one, get one referrals, even though there isn't inherent product network effects, they're still able to generate meaningful results off of the, and incentivize referring program.
turns.zh: 然后就非常强了。我觉得还有另一种情况，就算没有内在网络效应，推荐和病毒闭环也能奏效——就是如果你有一个特别被热爱的产品、特别被热爱的品牌。澳大利亚有一家公司我机会投资了，叫 Laika，做鲜食狗粮订阅，品牌极度被热爱，产品是高端的。所以他们能倚靠“给一个、得一个”的推荐机制，哪怕没有内在产品网络效应，依然能靠这个有激励的推荐计划产出可观的结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you talk about network effects, what does that mean to you? How would you define that briefly?
turns.zh: 你说网络效应的时候，对你来说是什么意思？你怎么简单定义一下？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah, to me, I mean, honestly I define it I think probably a pretty quintessential way, which is for every individual user, the utility that they derive from the product increases the more users there are on the platform. The expanded version of that is in a case of marketplaces. It may not be the bore users broadly speaking, but the more users in the markets that you care about, in the case of collaboration tools, it's not the more users in abstract terms. It's the more users within your team, the more users within your company, right? That correlates with your kind of the rise in your utility curve.
turns.zh: 对，对我来说，我定义的方式可能挺经典的：对每个个体用户来说，平台上的用户越多，他从产品里得到的效用就越大。更展开一点说，在 marketplace 的情况下，不是泛指“用户更多”，而是你所在意的市场里的用户更多；在协作工具的情况下，不是抽象地说“用户更多”，而是你团队里、你公司里的人更多，对吧？这就跟你的效用曲线上升对应上了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So if you have network effects, AKA if the product becomes more useful with more people or there's amazing word of mouth already, or there's collaboration, probably a good sign that you could lean into virality or maybe referrals. What about SEO?
turns.zh: 太好了。所以如果你有网络效应，也就是产品人越多越好用，或者已经有惊人的口碑，或者有协作属性，那大概是个好信号，说明你可以去倚重病毒传播或推荐。那 SEO 呢？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Oh, that's a good one. It's a very timely question because I actually in a process of helping a couple of my companies figure out if it's the right time to invest in SEO. So I've been sort of a forefront of taking exploratory meetings with agencies and SEO consultants and things like that. I mean, I would say the first thing to figure... I mean, there are a couple of pillars, because obviously we all know that SEO has a different return horizon than say paid acquisition. It's longer out. It's maybe six months is the earliest you can see results. Even then it's going to be a small trickle that compounds over time, if you're successful or you may spend three to six months leaning into an SEO strategy and then realize that it's not going to back out typically at least in historically a company probably isn't like Series B before it starts feeling like it passed a luxury of making these kind of medium to long term investments.
turns.zh: 哦，这个好。问题很应景，因为我其实正在帮几家我的公司判断现在是不是投资 SEO 的好时机。所以我正站在最前沿，跟一些代理商和 SEO 顾问开探索性的会。我的意思是，我想说的第一件事是……有几根支柱，因为显然我们都知道，SEO 的投资回报周期跟付费获客不一样，它更长。最早可能也要六个月才能看到结果。即使那时也只是很小的一股细流，会随时间复利式增长——如果你做得成的话；或者你可能花了三到六个月投入 SEO 策略，然后发现它回不来本，通常——至少历史上——一家公司大概要到 B 轮之后，才感觉有“奢侈”去做这种中长期的投入。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: But I think that's shifting right now, but that's maybe a topic for later or even for another bot but a lot of the strategies that I think we're reserved for Series B are trickling down to Series A companies because they have to diversify way for pay, but maybe more on that later. So I think with SEO, it's like the first pillar I would say is, do you have a unique angle when you take a look at the SEO landscape today, you look at editorial, the landscape, which is to how to searches and who are the players there and what kind of information is being offered? Do you have something unique to contribute to that conversation? Another thing if I have to do an audit checklist, another thing is, do you have a unique programmatic angle, right? For instance, Canva did dealt with templates. Who else is programmatic?
turns.zh: 但我觉得现在正在变化，不过那可能是后面再聊的话题，甚至换一期播客聊。很多原本留给 B 轮的策略，正在下探到 A 轮公司，因为他们必须给付费之外找条多元化的路。可能后面再细说。所以说到 SEO，我想第一根支柱是：你看待今天的 SEO 格局时，有没有独特的切入点？你看看编辑类内容、整个格局——大家都在搜什么、玩家是谁、提供的是什么信息？你能为这场对话贡献什么独特的东西？如果我要做个审计清单，另一项是：你有没有独特的程序化角度？比如 Canva 靠模板起家。还有谁在做程序化？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: CWELL, Redfit, obviously all the real estate, right? That's really strong-
turns.zh: Zillow、Redfin，显然还有所有房产类的，对，那很强——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Saint Pier.
turns.zh: Stripe，对。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Saint Pier, right. So do you have a programmatic angle and then understanding the competitive landscape or the other one is, do you have a unique data angle? So for instance, a company I work with called Monarch Money, which is in the personal finance management space. Think of it as a new and improved version of MIT. There is a lot of users are connecting accounts and you have a sense percenting patterns and things like that. Clearly there is a unique data, and so it's a question of, can you turn it into some kind of valuable organic search experience?
turns.zh: Stripe，对。所以你有没有程序化角度，然后理解竞争格局；还有一个是，你有没有独特的数据角度？比如我合作的一家叫 Monarch Money 的公司，在做个人财务管理，可以想成是 Mint 的升级版。很多用户在连账户，你能感知到消费模式之类的。显然这里有独特数据，所以问题是，你能不能把它变成某种有价值的自然搜索体验？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I won't go into too much detail in terms of what we're thinking of there, but that's another checkbox. If you can check two of those three boxes as a back of the envelope framework, you may be in good shape. And then it's a question of like, "How can you lower the cost of experimentation SEO as much as possible?" I think as a rule of thumb, if you can time box it to three months, what can I do at the end of three months? Is this likely to work or not?
turns.zh: 关于我们在想什么我就不细说了，但那是另一个勾选项。如果你三个勾能勾中两个，作为粗略框架，你可能状态不错。然后问题就变成：“怎么尽可能降低 SEO 实验的成本？”我的经验法则是，如果你能把试错时间框在三个月内——三个月结束时我能判断，这到底有没有可能成？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Couple follow up questions.
turns.zh: 太好了。几个追问。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One is SEO feels like this dark art where you need some SEO wizard to come help you through this.
turns.zh: 一个是，SEO 感觉像一门黑魔法，你需要某个 SEO 巫师来帮你走完这个过程。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you suggest companies find somebody or work with an agency or something else? What's your general feeling on SEO versus some other route?
turns.zh: 你建议公司去找个人、跟代理商合作，还是别的什么？你对 SEO 跟其他路线的整体感受是什么？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I think SEO is pretty specialized skill set. There are some basic principles that always hold like best content wins and don't do shady back linking and make sure that you're on page. SEO is good and your pages are easily crawl, but I feel like everybody knows that. And where the winners are determined are between the lines. Better than a sports' analogy? Maybe you can.
turns.zh: 我觉得 SEO 是个相当专业化的技能。有些基本原则永远成立，比如“最好的内容会赢”、别做 shady 的垃圾外链、确保你的 on-page SEO 到位、页面容易被抓取，但我觉得这些大家都懂。胜负是在字里行间决定的。比体育类比好一点？也许你可以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Between the lines. I don't know what that comes from.
turns.zh: 字里行间。我不知道那是哪来的说法。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: But anyway, what I mean is that there is a lot of more nuance, SEO developments and angles, where I think is where the opportunity really lies to differentiate yourself. And that requires keeping up with the latest algorithm changes. It's very hard to do that unless you are specializing in the art where the black magic of SEO, and so that's why I think getting an outside resource at least for an audit is really helpful. Now, whether it's a boutique agency or a solo consultant, I think that's more circumstantial, but I've found at least with the companies that I've worked with, if we wanted to quickly vet the SEO opportunity, I can do it in a very kind of amateur, at an amateur level.
turns.zh: 但总之，我的意思是，SEO 有很多更细微的发展角度，我觉得真正的差异化机会就在那儿。这需要紧跟最新的算法变化。除非你专门钻研这门黑魔法，否则很难做到，所以我认为至少做一次外部审计、找个外部资源是真的很管用。现在，是找精品代理商还是独立顾问，我觉得更看具体情况，但我发现，至少在我合作过的公司里，如果我们想快速验证 SEO 机会，我可以用很业余的水平先做个初步判断。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Plug things into similar web and try to figure out the right option is there, but you can get these relatively inexpensive audits done from companies that you can then choose. Do I hire them to help with my SEO or not? But I think that audit is usually a very good use of time because they have templates. So what they can turn around for five to 10K would take you many, many human hours to try to pull together yourself.
turns.zh: 把东西丢进 SimilarWeb 之类，试着找出合适的选项，但你可以花相对便宜的钱做这些审计，然后你再来选：我要不要雇他们帮我做 SEO？但我觉得那个审计通常非常值得花时间，因为他们有模板。他们花 5 千到 1 万美元能交付的东西，你自己要花无数个人力小时才能拼凑出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Are there agencies that you want to name that people can go check out or would you prefer just to keep it from having-
turns.zh: 太好了。有没有你愿意点名的代理商，大家可以去看看？还是你更倾向于不——

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I'll give one plug.
turns.zh: 我给一个推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I think one of the most innovative, disciplined first principles SEO thinkers and I have met is Ethan Smith from Graphite. It's not for everyone. It's a pretty high end SEO shell. So I wouldn't send the Series a company there, but Ethan also produces a lot of resources and what they've been focusing on at Graphite lately has been actually automating a lot of their work and turning it into SAS. So I don't know how far along they are, but you could probably already get into some of the betas from the tools that they're offering.
turns.zh: 我觉得我见过最有创意、最有纪律、最第一性原理的 SEO 思考者之一，是 Graphite 的 Ethan Smith。这不是给所有人准备的，是个相当高端的 SEO 精品。所以我不会把 A 轮公司往那儿送，但 Ethan 也产出很多资源，他们最近在 Graphite 重点做的是把他们很多工作自动化、做成 SaaS。所以我不知道进展到哪了，但你应该已经能进他们一些工具的 beta 了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. I'm going to try to get Ethan on this podcast.
turns.zh: 赞。我会想办法把 Ethan 请上这档播客。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've seen his stuff and it's awesome.
turns.zh: 我看过他的东西，太厉害了。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah. He is a math scientist when it comes to SEO. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。他在 SEO 这件事上就是个数学科学家。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We need those. We need math scientist on ship.
turns.zh: 我们需要这种人。我们需要数学科学家上船。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So we've talked about virality talked about SEO, paid. Imagine that's pretty straightforward if your LTV are high enough and you can pay back ads on those, then that's where you go. Imagine everyone can try it. Doesn't work for everyone. What if yeah, anything you want to add there?
turns.zh: 好。我们聊了病毒传播，聊了 SEO，聊了付费。我猜付费很直白——如果你的 LTV 足够高，能用广告回本，那就去投。我猜谁都能试。不是对谁都管用。关于付费你还有什么想补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I mean, there's a lot. There's a lot. I mean, I don't know how deep you want to go down the paid rabbit hole because it's changing. It's probably the most affected growth bucket in light of the market turbulence, the venture sentiment shifting. I've seen paying acquisition strategies at budgets. They are at the brunt of that fallout. And so the question is where do you want to go there?
turns.zh: 嗯，可说的太多了。我不知道你想往付费这个兔子洞钻多深，因为它在变。受市场动荡、风投情绪转向的影响，它大概是被冲击最大的增长板块。我看到付费获客策略和预算首当其冲。所以问题你想往哪走？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That's a really good topic. I was saving that for later, but let's chat it better right now.
turns.zh: 对。这话题真好。我本来留到后面，但现在聊更好。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine part of this is Apple's tracking changes too.
turns.zh: 我猜这部分也跟苹果改成把归因更新有关。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I guess my big question is paid still lucrative and a good path for many companies is like 50% of the time less effective. How do you see that shifting recently? And how should people think about paid in the consumer subscription startup?
turns.zh: 所以我的大问题是：付费现在还有利可图、还是很多公司的好路径吗？是“一半时间效果差了”那种程度吗？你最近怎么看这个变化？消费级订阅创业公司该怎么思考付费？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Well, I think in the short term, let's break it down into phases. I think in the short term paid acquisition and just paid media dollars are contracted and we're seeing it already with Metas advertising revenue, Snaps advertising revenue. There's clearly a global contraction happening to paid media budgets. A big part of it is because all of a sudden the definition of efficient acquisition and good payback windows is shifting. So before for a consumer subscription company, 12 month payback was decent. Now it's like, you better pay back your paid media in six months or less. That's the sentiment.
turns.zh: 我觉得短期来看，我们把它分阶段看。短期里，付费获客、整个付费媒体预算是在收缩的，我们在 Meta 的广告收入、Snap 的广告收入上已经看到了。显然全球范围内付费媒体预算都在收缩。很大一部分原因是，突然之间“高效获客”和“好的回本周期”的定义在变。以前对消费级订阅公司来说，12 个月回本算不错。现在是：你最好能在六个月或更短把付费媒体回本。这就是现在的情绪。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: So the thought is reaction is like anything that's more than six months we're well board of six months, we're cutting that and so there's that. Then there is just less tolerance for ambiguity and attribution when the sentiment is like, "Let's grow at [inaudible 00:25:38]. Grow at all costs." If you can't attribute things perfectly, that's okay. Now it's like, especially with venture back companies, you have to have two plus years of runway, managers burn a lot more diligently now. And so whatever you can't attribute to sales sue like, "That shits got to go." I don't know if we can curse on the pod or not.

turns.en: Only available-

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen

turns.en: At least.

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: All right. Way loud. All right. But anyways, yeah. So I think there is a short term contraction. However, that opens up an opportunity for smart kind of attribution investments. So you're seeing an emergence of some interesting attribution related attribution for incrementality related products. A couple that I personally started exploring and looking into, and then you just see a lot more heads of growth, heads of user acquisition, thinking about attribution in building their attribution stacks. And so I think that once we settle into some kind of new normal, which is going to be a combination of just better attribution stack on average for companies combined with just the level of acceptance, that attribution will never be as good as it maybe once was. We're going to probably get hit. Come out of that and you'll see paid budgets start making their way back. But even right now, during contraction, there are going to be some winners.
turns.zh: 好。大声点。好。但总之，对，我觉得短期是收缩。不过，这也给聪明的归因投资打开了机会。所以你会看到一些有意思的、跟归因和增量性相关的产品冒出来。我自己最近开始接触和研究的就有几个，而且你会看到越来越多增长负责人、用户获客负责人在思考归因、搭建他们的归因技术栈。所以我觉得，等我们落到某种“新常态”——它会是“公司平均有更好的归因技术栈”加上“大家接受归因永远不可能像以前那么好”这两者的结合——我们会熬过去，然后你会看到付费预算开始回流。但即使现在收缩期，也会有赢家。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: The companies that had strong cash positions, have strong unit economics, strong paid back periods already like Grammarly, Canva to name two that I know personally. A couple of others or many others probably, they're going to be winners because all of a sudden, if previously they were competing with companies who were nowhere as efficient as them, but for whatever reason had the green light to keep spending, now all of those are going to pull back their budgets. And so those that have been disciplined, have the instrumentation to track things better than average. They're going to benefit from decreased competition on app platforms, decreasing CPMs, et cetera. So they're going to do winners for sure.
turns.zh: 那些现金状况强、单位经济模型健康、回本周期本来就短的公司，比如 Grammarly、Canva，这两个是我个人认识的。还有其他一些，他们会是赢家。因为突然之间，如果以前他们要跟那些效率远不如他们的公司竞争，但那些公司不知为啥拿到了绿灯继续烧钱，现在那些全都会收缩预算。而一直自律、有更好的埋点来追踪数据的公司，会从应用商店平台竞争减少、CPM 下降等等里受益。所以他们肯定是赢家。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Haven't heard this perspective. It's so interesting that the fact that it's gotten harder, it's creating new opportunities for companies to do it better and more intelligently. You said you mentioned a couple tools products that you found to be potentially helpful in this. Is there anything you could mention there?
turns.zh: 哇。没听过这个视角。真有意思——正因为变难了，反而给公司创造了把这件事做得更好、更聪明的机会。你提到你发现几个可能在这个方向有用的工具或产品。有没有什么可以点名的？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I mentioned a couple that I've kind of connected with in the last couple of months. So first of all, Media Mix Modeling is making a comeback, which is something that kind of got popularized in the math meant kind of advertising era of the fifties, pre-digital, and that's how that was the piece of the methodology. I can't speak of the specifics there. The science is a little bit out of depth there, but it was basically a way to use some data to determine a budget allocation across channels at the time was probably newspapers and billboards, et etcetera.
turns.zh: 对。我提几个最近两三个月联系过的。首先，媒体组合建模（Media Mix Modeling）正在复兴，这个方法在五六十年代、数字时代之前的广告黄金期流行过，那曾是方法论的一部分。具体细节我说不好。那门科学我有点超出能力范围，但它基本是一种用数据来决定跨渠道预算分配的方法——当时大概是报纸和广告牌之类的。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: It was leveraging data to some extent. You would were doing it maybe on a quarterly basis. And then you would only update it every quarter. There was no way with media mix modeling. There was no way to adjust budget in quarter because you weren't getting the data feedback loop that frequently. But media mix modeling is now making a comeback because there are so many offline channels that are part of folks channel portfolio today and that plus a lot of the online channels are becoming less trackable like Meta for instance, with the iOS 14 shift. And so Media Mix Modeling is going to comeback and the company that's leading the charge of bringing the Media Mix Modeling methodology of the traditional advertising era and ushering it into the digital world is a company called the Recast.
turns.zh: 它当时在一定程度上用到了数据。你可能一个季度做一次，然后整个季度只更新一次。媒体组合建模没法在季度内调预算，因为你拿不到那么频繁的数据反馈。但现在媒体组合建模在复兴，因为今天很多人的渠道组合里有大量线下渠道，再加上很多线上渠道变得不那么可追踪了，比如 Meta 在 iOS 14 之后。所以媒体组合建模要回来了，而把传统广告时代的这套方法论带进数字世界、引领这股潮流的公司，叫 Recast。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Recast.
turns.zh: Recast。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Recast. Yeah. So I've heard really good things. I haven't tried them with any of my companies yet, but there are a couple that are on the horizon hopefully.
turns.zh: 对，Recast。我听到的评价都很不错。我还没在我的任何公司上试过，但有几家在 horizon 上，希望会试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Double click there for a moment. Is that still useful if you're not doing TV and other forms of advertising?
turns.zh: 在那多说一点。如果你不做电视和其他形式的广告，它还有用吗？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I think it's still-
turns.zh: 我觉得还是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're just doing-
turns.zh: 你只是做——

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's useful if you're spending a considerable amount, what's considerable, I'd say worth of a hundred thousand a month update media. And if you have some level of channel complexity, so you're not just like a Google Go or a Facebook, but maybe you're on three plus the channels. Then I think it still makes sense. The other ones in the incremental space, they have very different methodologists actually, because at end of the day, this might be obvious to folks, but maybe some will find value.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得有用，前提是你花的钱够多——什么叫够多？我说是每月值得在媒体上花十万以上的时候。而且你有一定程度的渠道复杂度，也就是说你不只是 Google 或 Facebook 一个渠道，而是三个以上。那我觉得它仍有意义。增量性领域里其他的公司，方法其实很不一样，因为归根结底，这点大家可能明白，但也许有人会觉得有价值。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Click based attribution or the digital attribution were all fawning over cookie based and click based, a real parameter based attribution. It never demonstrated a causal relationship between our media spend and business results. It was only good for correlative insights. And the only way to determine causality is through real controlled experiments, randomized control experiments through incrementality testing, which is typically really hard to do cleanly and also companies have always been often wary about doing it because you have to turn off a channel potentially in a key demo and you're like, "Yeah." The benefit is to learning of whether it's actually incremental, but the cost or the sales that I will lose today. But the only way to really know how effective your paid media is through ongoing incrementality testing. So there are two companies that are addressing that. Two that I'm excited about. One is measured, can be found, measured.call, amazing domain name.
turns.zh: 基于点击的归因、或者说数字归因，我们曾经全都迷恋基于 cookie、基于点击、基于真实参数（real parameter）的归因。它从来没能证明媒体支出和业务结果之间的因果关系。它只能给相关性层面的洞察。而确定因果关系的唯一方式，是通过真正的受控实验、随机对照实验、通过增量性测试——这通常很难干净地做，而且公司一直往往对它很警惕，因为你可能得在某个关键人群里关掉一个渠道，你会想“嗯”。好处是能学到它到底是不是增量的，但代价是今天会损失的销售。但要知道你的付费媒体到底多有效，唯一的办法就是持续做增量性测试。所以有两家公司在解决这个问题。我挺兴奋的两家。一家叫 Measured，域名 measured.com，绝妙的域名。

The more people can actually make change. I had a couple questions here that I wanted to follow up on. One is founders might be listening to this and they're like, "Amazing. Okay, we're going to grow. There's three ways to grow. Let's do it all. Get someone on SEO to get Jane on paid. Let's get Fred on virality."
turns.zh: 对。我喜欢。这很棒。这正是人们需要的。他们就想知道：“好，那我到底该做什么？”所以越清楚该实际试什么、怎么解决这些问题，人们就越能真正做出改变。我有几个想追问的问题。一个是，创始人可能正在听，然后想：“太棒了。好，我们要增长了。有三条增长路径。全做。找个人做 SEO，让 Jane 做付费，让 Fred 做病毒传播。”

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So in your experience, is it smart to focus on one and then expand down the road or try them all see which one works best? How do you advise companies think about these options?
turns.zh: 所以根据你的经验，是聪明地先聚焦一个、以后再扩展，还是全都试试、看哪个最好？你怎么建议公司思考这些选项？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I would say focus paired with rapid iterations, right? With limited resources. Naturally you have to practice some form of essentialism and ruthless prioritization, but at the same time, the clock is always ticking. You can not burn. That there is a finite number of tries that you have at finding what works, right? What's going to help you unlock the next level of growth, get to the next funding round, extend your runway. And so I think either one taking to an extreme focus or trying multiple things is not a good thing. And just in case, it's not obvious if you focus on one thing and it ends up being the wrong thing, you've wasted really valuable time and now you have so much less time left to find something that does work. Spreading yourself very thin oftentimes in the early stage companies, it's one person who's in charge of all of growth, but they also have some other kind of responsibilities like maybe ops and customer success.
turns.zh: 我会说“聚焦 + 快速迭代”，对吧？资源有限，你自然得做某种本质主义（essentialism）和毫不留情的优先级排序，但同时，时钟一直在走。你没法无限烧。你能找到“什么管用”的尝试次数是有限的，对吧？什么能帮你解锁下一层增长、撑到下一轮融资、延长跑道。所以我觉得，把聚焦走到极端、或者什么都试，都不是好事。以防不明显：如果你聚焦一件事、结果它是错的，你浪费了宝贵时间，现在你找对的东西的时间就少得多了。而在早期公司，摊得太薄往往是一个人负责全部增长，还兼着别的责任，比如运营和客户成功。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: If you get them to try five different things, they may not try them anyone individually fully enough, because I like to say the only thing that's worse than a channel or a tactic that you tried not working. The only thing that's worse now is when you didn't give it the appropriate shot and you pretty much surely or erroneously concluded that it doesn't work. And it's remarkable how often you find that to be the case when I talk to companies, "Oh, YouTube, we tried it doesn't work." I'm like, "Okay, can I see what you've tried?" And then you look at it and you're like, "Oh, this thing was not designed to even have a shot at working from the get go." So to answer your question, I think it's focus with some guard rails so that you know exactly when it's time to move on to the next thing.
turns.zh: 如果你让他试五件不同的事，可能哪一件都没试透，因为我想说，比“试了一个渠道或打法却没效果”更糟的，只有一种情况，就是你没给它应有的机会，就基本确定、或者错误地断定它不行。我在跟公司聊的时候，经常发现这种事——“哦，YouTube我们试过了，没用。”我就说：“好啊，让我看看你们试了什么？”然后一看就会发现：“哦，这东西从一开始就没被设计成有机会跑通的样子。”所以回答你的问题，我觉得是带着护栏的聚焦，这样你清楚地知道什么时候该换到下一件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This might be too hard to answer in a chat like this, but do you have any guidance for how to know when you've gone far enough? I imagine there's a lot nuance and detail there. Is there anything that you could share?
turns.zh: 这个问题在这种聊天里可能太难回答了，但你有没有什么指引，让人知道什么时候算“试够了”？我猜这里面有很多细微差别和细节。有没有什么能分享的？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Love the question. It's very thought provoking. I think with some tactics and some channels you can fairly objectively create some test guard rails where it's like, if it's YouTube, we know kind of minimum number of impressions that you got to get. Try two to three creative angles. Here's the click through rates range that you're looking for. If you get within these ranges on these KPIs, keep going. If you don't, abandon.
turns.zh: 喜欢这个问题。很有启发性。我觉得对一些打法和渠道，你可以相当客观地设定一些测试护栏，比如：如果是 YouTube，我们知道大概得拿到的最低曝光量。试两到三个创意角度。这是你要的点击率区间。如果这几个 KPI 你能进这个区间，就继续；进不了，就放弃。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I think that's important to also know that abandonment doesn't mean we will never revisit it again, right? It just means that because every time you're evaluating, the concept of sunk cost. So you have these periodic, I think periods of reevaluation where it's like, "Okay, did we try enough? Is this more art than science frankly." It's like, "What's the incremental lift for us as a team to try to experiment with the next phase of this channel or this tactic? What is the opportunity cost of that? What are the other high profile things that we could be trying?" You were right and save this topic too hard to answer in this format, but I would break things down maybe into two types. There are some channels or tactics where you can objectively figure out som guard rails for when it's showing promise or not, because you can pull benchmarks on good click through rates and things like that. Then there are other tactics where you just have to exercise more judgment outside of benchmarks.
turns.zh: 我觉得同样重要的是要知道，放弃不代表我们永远不再碰它，对吧？只是因为每次你在评估时，都要考虑沉没成本。所以你会有这些定期的重新评估期，比如：“好，我们试够了吗？这说到底是艺术还是科学。”比如：“作为团队，去试这个渠道或打法的下一阶段，能带来多少增量提升？机会成本是什么？我们有哪些其他高优先级的事可以试？”你说得对，这个话题在这种形式里确实太难回答，但我会把事情分成两类。有些渠道或打法，你能客观地定出护栏，判断它有没有希望，因为你能拉到好的点击率之类的基准。另一些打法，你就得在基准之外更多地靠判断。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. That was actually really valuable and very challenging question to try to summarize quickly so thank you. One more quick question along these lines. So you talked about these three broad ways companies grow. Oftentimes a couple of them work, something I've seen and I'm curious if you agree, usually one is like 80% of your growth and then you layer on a couple more to optimize. Is that what you see?
turns.zh: 对，对。这其实很有价值，而且是个很难快速总结的问题，所以谢谢你。沿着这个方向再一个快速问题。你说了公司增长的这三大类方式。经常是两三种都管用，我观察到的、也好奇你认不认同的是：通常其中一种占了你增长的 80%，然后你再叠加上另外几种来做优化。你看到的是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yes. I think companies that we know and admire and reference in case studies or in podcast, such as this one. From the outside looking in, you oftentimes assume that it's a highly diversified growth engine. I have to say it's often not the case. Definitely the 80/20 applies. There is a kind of strategy that's working overwhelmingly well, and there is a scramble internally to minimize reliance on that one thing. And on the discover slash on the walk, the next step function, the next growth horizon. In the case of Grammarly, it was performance marketing kind of over reliance on performance marketing during part of the company's life cycle. And so it was like, "Okay, this thing is working." It's efficient so you don't want to stop pouring fire on it, but you're also thinking months and years ahead, what kind of risk does it open you up to?
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得我们熟知、在案例研究或播客（比如这期）里引用的那些公司，从外面看，你往往假设它们有一套高度多元化的增长引擎。我得说，通常并不是。80/20 法则肯定适用。有一个策略好用得出奇，而公司内部则在手忙脚乱地想减少对这一件事的依赖，同时去寻找下一个阶跃、下一个增长地平线。在 Grammarly 的例子里，是效果营销——在公司生命周期的某个阶段，过度依赖效果营销。所以就是：“好，这东西管用。”它高效，所以你不想停火，但你也得往前看几个月、几年，这让你暴露在什么样的风险里？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: And so there is a scramble to fight and at Grammarly, it's been successful there. With Canva, it was the SEO angle. So for them, that was working really well, which is more defensible than paid. That's sort of long tail programmatic SEO angle, but look, you're always susceptible to Google algorithm updates and so how do you derisk yourself from that? But to your point, yes. And I think that surprising thing to people probably is that it's also the case with some later stage companies. It's not just early stage companies that are kind of one trick pulleys. Sometimes it's later stage companies as well.
turns.zh: 所以在 Grammarly 内部有一场“去依赖化”的挣扎，而且成功了。在 Canva 那里，是 SEO 角度。对他们来说那招特别好用，比付费更可防守——就是那种长尾程序化 SEO 角度，但你看，你永远会受到 Google 算法更新的冲击，所以你怎么给自己去风险？但如你所说，是的。而且我觉得让人意外的大概是：一些更后期的公司也是这样。不只有早期公司是“一招鲜”。有时候后期公司也是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This makes me think about is there's kind of these three phases to growth. There's the kickstart phase where you're just doing a bunch of stuff, trying to get things moving. Then there's that you discover your first main growth engine and then there's layer on additional engines because you want to diversify.
turns.zh: 这让我想到，增长大概有三个阶段。有启动阶段，你东试西试，想让事情动起来。然后你发现了第一个主要的增长引擎，然后是叠加额外的引擎，因为你想要多元化。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yep. And one interesting, what I believe is an interesting period and a lot of it is gut feel, right? And I try to direct companies. I encounter sometimes early stage companies is when one thing is working well and they're already worried about over reliance and they're starting to talk about diversification and I come in all the times and I see showing up in their OKRs. I come, "No, no. Too early. I'm glad that you're such a forward thinker. Put all of your energy. Sure, this one tactic is accounting for say 80 plus percent of your new user acquisition, but your user acquisition is still small. So don't get distracted with diversification. We'll get there. Lean more into this, hit this growth rates, stand this up. Build this into a real strategic advantages thing that's working."
turns.zh: 对。有一个我认为是挺有意思的阶段，而且很大程度靠直觉，对吧？我试着引导公司。我有时候遇到早期公司，一件事正用得好，他们已经在担心过度依赖，开始聊多元化，我在他们的 OKR 里看到这个。我就会去说：“不不，太早了。我很高兴你是这么有远见的人。把全部精力放上去。没错，这一个打法占了你新增用户获取的 80% 以上，但你的用户获取总量还很小。所以别被多元化分心。那一步会到的。再往这个上加力，把增长率打出来，把这个立起来。把正在管用的东西，建成真正的战略优势。”

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: So I actually have to talk them out, focusing on diversification too early. Contrast that with some later stage companies for who are... At scale, I know 50 plus million ARR, 90 plus percent reliant on a single acquisition channel, which just mire with risk and diversification is a blind spot for them. And then with those, I have to be like, "Hey y'all. Here's the risk that you're carrying. Let's start carving out bandwidth resources to try to go and explore these other channels with tactics."
turns.zh: 所以我其实得劝他们别太早聚焦多元化。对比一些后期公司——到了规模，我知道有 5000 万美元以上 ARR、90% 以上依赖单一获客渠道的，那简直是风险的温床，多元化对他们是个盲点。而对那些公司，我得说：“嘿，各位。这是你们背的风险。我们开始拨出带宽和资源，去试着探索其他渠道和打法吧。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such an important point. It reminds me Casey has this hilarious line that he uses that the money's always in the banana stand or there's always more money in the banana stand from [inaudible 00:41:59] development. That basically your growth is probably going to come from the same place it's already come from.
turns.zh: 这点太重要了。让我想起 Casey 有个超好笑的说法，他说“钱永远在香蕉摊里”（the money's always in the banana stand），或者说“香蕉摊里永远有更多钱”，来自《发展受阻》（Arrested Development）。大意就是，你的增长大概率会来自它已经来的那个地方。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that you shouldn't take that for granted. And you should put most of your efforts into continuing to optimize that versus being distracted by, "Oh, let's do SEO now."
turns.zh: 而且你不该把这当成理所当然。你应该把大部分精力放在继续优化它上面，而不是被“哦，我们现在做 SEO 吧”分心。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I see that argument for sure.
turns.zh: 这个论点我当然认同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you mentioned at this point about how later stage growth strategies are starting to move earlier into growth strategy planning. I'd love to hear more on that.
turns.zh: 你前面提到，后期增长策略正在更早地进入增长战略规划。我想多听听这个。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah. Let me expand on that in the world that we lived in last 18 months, or let's say up until say three to five months ago. We were living in a world where funding was abundant and plentiful, startups were conditions to think that they could raise twice a year. Valuations were quite toppling within a year. You raise in January and then you raise in November and your valuation five X. And so companies were coming off of these ridiculous Series As of 15 to 25 million dollar As and they were like, "We got to grow as quickly as possible. What can we activate to give us immediate return?" And the answer is almost always paid. That one going to give you, especially if you're think you want to go back to raising less than 12 months later, that forces you to focus on very kind of short term tactics, short payoff tactics.
turns.zh: 好。让我展开说。在我们过去 18 个月、或者说直到三四个月前所处的世界里，资金充裕、到处都是。创业公司习惯了以为自己一年能融两轮。估值一年内翻好几倍。你一月融一轮，十一月再融一轮，估值翻五倍。所以公司从这些离谱的 A 轮——1500 到 2500 万美元的 A 轮——出来，就想：“我们得尽快增长。有什么能立刻带来回报的？”答案几乎总是付费。因为如果你想着不到 12 个月就要再去融，那会逼你聚焦在非常短期的战术、短期回本的打法上。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: And so things that SEO, there was no room to think about that for early stage companies. Because payoff is going to come maybe in 12 months in terms of meaningful payoff. We care about getting to the next round and maximizing our valuation between now and then. SEO is for the grown up companies. When we're that we could think about it. And they were getting the reinforcement from everywhere, from peers, from VCs. It's like it's growth, growth, growth. The growth at any cause.
turns.zh: 所以像 SEO 这种事，早期公司根本没空间去想。因为它的回报可能要 12 个月才来得明显。我们关心的是撑到下一轮、在期间把估值最大化。SEO 是给“长大的公司”准备的。等我们长大了再想。而且他们从各方——同行、VC——都在得到强化：增长、增长、增长，不惜一切代价增长。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I think what happened now and we'll see where things stabilized because I think we're still in the midst of a little bit of chaos. What's happening now is the same VCs are saying, "Okay, it's now survival." You have to extend your runway, minimize burn, high burning if you have to. And all of a sudden growth, whether explicitly or via inference becomes kind of a secondary objective, especially for all these companies that are far from being cash flow positive. They have to figure out how to stay alive, but not have to go back to the market and be sort of a victim of shitty terms. And so I feel this is me extrapolating because venture capitalist didn't actually tell me this, but I'm extrapolating that growth is a secondary objective now. It's really focusing on sustainability due to economics, accepting your runway control your destiny, getting to default life.
turns.zh: 我觉得现在发生的事——还得看局势怎么稳住，因为我觉得我们还在一片混乱中间。现在发生的是，同一批 VC 在说：“好，现在是求生存。”你得延长跑道、减少烧钱，该烧就烧。突然之间，增长不管明说还是暗示，都变成了次要目标，尤其对那些离现金流为正还差得远的公司。他们得想办法活下来，又不必被迫回到市场上、沦为糟糕条款的受害者。所以我觉得——这是我外推的，因为 VC 没真的告诉我——但我外推的结论是，增长现在是次要目标了。真正聚焦的是因为经济而追求可持续性、掌控你的跑道、掌握自己的命运、达到“默认活着”（default alive）的状态。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: And all of a sudden it's like, "Okay. Plus paid is a lot less attractive now. Can't afford to be acquiring users at like LTV cap one to one." That's now a no-no. And so SEO is now becoming more attractive because once you got your burn under control and you're thinking, "Okay, we saved all this money by reducing our paid budget. We're cutting it entirely. How do we put some of those resources back to work?" And all of a sudden SEO starts looking a lot more lucrative because it's almost like you took the urgency of grow at any cost in the next six months, you took that out of the equation. So now it's like we're in a position where we don't have to go back to raising 12, 18, 24 months. We have 18, 24 months worth of runway and now companies are starting to think more in terms of building more sort of sustainable and defensible growth initiatives.
turns.zh: 突然之间就变成了：“好，而且付费现在吸引力差多了。不能再以 LTV 一比一这种回本方式去获客了。”那现在是禁忌。所以 SEO 现在变得更有吸引力，因为一旦你把烧钱控制住，想着“好，我们通过砍付费预算省下了这么多钱，全砍了。我们怎么把其中一些资源重新用起来？”突然之间 SEO 看起来诱人多了，因为就等于你把“六个月里不惜一切代价增长”的那种紧迫感从方程里拿掉了。所以现在是：我们不用在 12、18、24 个月里回去融。我们有 18、24 个月的跑道，现在公司开始更多地从建立更可持续、更可防守的增长举措的角度去思考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. And as much as people may want to do SEO, like we talked about earlier, doesn't mean they will be able to pull it off because there's these things that have to be approved for your type of company and-
turns.zh: 着迷。而且尽管大家可能想做 SEO，就像我们前面聊的，不代表他们能做成，因为得满足你们这类公司要具备的那些前提——

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Going back to point you made earlier about paid being a really interesting opportunity right now because it's become harder. Would you say generally you're kind of like pro, tri paid, go paid be in this time because I'm finding a lot of startups are like, "Oh, we can't do paid anymore. We're trying all these other approaches to grow." Is that like alpha right now? Start thinking about paid in a creative way and maybe this is going to be a huge advantage.
turns.zh: 对。回到你前面说的，付费因为变难了，现在反而成了很有意思的机会。你会不会总体上说，你现在是“挺付费、去投付费”这种态度？因为我发现很多创业公司像“哦，我们不能做付费了，我们在试所有别的路径来增长。”这是不是当下的 alpha（超额收益）？开始用有创意的方式思考付费，也许这会是个巨大优势。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: So there are two pieces to do paid. I mean I'm oversimplifying, but I think people will hopefully appreciate the over the oversimplification. Number one, because it actually drives returns at efficient unit economic, whatever that may mean for your company, your business, your industry. The other way to do it is because it's a very quick way to get learnings on messaging and positioning on designs on features. You're thinking of launching et cetera, right? It's hard to get faster learnings at scale than A/B testing headlines, Google search or whatever. I think the problem that I find is when a company can't have which camper in or where they try to say that they're in both, but really it's like, "Okay, you're funneling a hundred K a month." It's super inefficient and they're not even running experiments to actually get the learnings. I can assess the company, even if I don't download the industry as well, based on just seeing their funnel performance, their conversion rates, their retention curves, their LTDs, understanding their churn.
turns.zh: 做付费有两部分。我有点过度简化了，但希望大家能欣赏这种简化。第一，因为它真的能在健康的单位经济下带来回报——不管对你的公司、生意、行业意味着什么。第二种做法是因为它是快速获得关于信息传达、定位、设计、功能的学习的方式。你想发个新东西之类的，对吧？在规模上，很难有比在 Google 搜索上 A/B 测试标题更快的学习了。我觉得我遇到的问题在于：当一家公司不知道自己属于哪种阵营，或者想说两者都是，但其实就像“好，你一个月烧十万刀”，效率低得要死，而且他们连实验都不跑来获取学习。我甚至不用特别懂那个行业，光看他们的漏斗表现、转化率、留存曲线、LTV、理解他们的流失，就能评估这家公司。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I could say whether they stand the chance at making paid work as a former strategy. So not just the learning mechanism, not just the kind of a feedback engine, but actually a profitable at delivering acquisition channel or strategy. And if I see that they're not there because the funnel doesn't convert well, the users don't retain the LTDs are too low. Then I say, "Hey, it's not time for paid. Maybe car on a little bit of budget if you want to quickly test positioning and things like that. But it's just too soon." But instead I encounter a company that's really healthy conversion rates, strong LTDs. I do a little bit of competitor research and I can see where the opportunities are, which channels are less saturated than others. Then I may say, "Hey, it's worth it. It's worth a go." And also just seeing the bigger picture of their financial health, how much runway do you have? What does your monthly burn look like?
turns.zh: 我能判断他们有没有机会把付费做成一种正经策略。不只是学习机制、不只是反馈引擎，而是真正能盈利的获客渠道或策略。如果我看到他们还没到那一步——因为漏斗转化不好、用户不留存、LTV 太低——我就会说：“嘿，还没到付费的时候。如果你想快速测一下定位和之类的，可以留一点点预算。但真的太早了。”而如果我遇到一家转化率高、LTV 强的公司，我做点竞品研究，能看到机会在哪、哪些渠道没那么饱和，那我可能会说：“嘿，值得，值得一试。”还有就是要看他们财务健康的全貌——你有多少跑道？每月烧多少？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right? Because paids like cash going out the door and it will return hopefully at some point might be six months might be a year, and so that's a real constraint. You mentioned onboarding and funnel conversion. Two questions there. One, do you have a heuristic of here's good for conversion rates? Is there something that you think about there that you could share or is it very case dependent?
turns.zh: 对吧？因为付费就是现金往外流，希望某天能回来，可能是六个月可能是一年，所以这是个真实的约束。你提到了上手流程和漏斗转化。在那有两个问题。一，你有没有个经验法则，比如“转化率到这就算好”？你有没有什么可以分享的，还是说非常看具体情况？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I think it's case dependent, but yeah, it is. It's not case dependent. It's category dependent. So it's not that every company is so case, but it's like, we got to know about what buckets we're talking about. I will say that... Let's say we talk about prosumer premium SAS, ala Grammarly, ala Canva, Whimsical, InVideo, things like that. Yeah. I can confidently say a healthy website visit to a free user, a free account creation conversion rate. It's probably in that 20 to 35% range.
turns.zh: 我觉得看具体情况，但也不全是。是看品类，不是每家公司都那么“具体情况”，而是我们得知道在说哪类桶。我会说……比如说我们聊专业消费者（prosumer）高端 SaaS，像 Grammarly、Canva、Whimsical、InVideo 这种。对，我可以自信地说，一个健康的“网站访问 → 免费用户/免费账号创建”转化率，大概在 20% 到 35% 这个区间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: From landing on the site to signing up?
turns.zh: 从落地网站到注册？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: From landing on site to a free user at scale. Earlier stage, you have strong product market fit with some kind of small audience segment that conversion can be 40 to 50%, but as you go broader, it'll probably asymptote at like 25, 30%. What about a conversion if you're premium from a free user to a premium account or paying account? I think anything under 5% is not going to work long term, regardless of how big your top of funnel is. You may get the soft point, but for you to remain an independent company continuously growing pre IPO, I don't think it's going to happen. It's got to be north of 5%, ideally like more than 7%.
turns.zh: 从落地网站到免费用户，在规模上。更早阶段，如果你在某个小受众段有强产品市场契合，转化率能到 40% 到 50%，但越铺广，大概会渐近到 25%、30%。那从免费用户到付费/高级账号的转化呢？我觉得任何低于 5% 的长期都撑不住，不管你的漏斗顶部多大。你可能短期拿到软点，但要想作为一家独立公司持续增长到上市前，我觉得不会发生。它必须高于 5%，理想是 7% 以上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Super handy. On the onboarding point, what's your thoughts on investing in onboarding and that part foe of how often is that a fruitful area of investment?
turns.zh: 哇。超实用。关于上手流程这点，你怎么看投上手流程，这部分通常有多大概率是个有产出的投入领域？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Almost always. A lot of my work is in that sort of a prosumer space. So the products tend to be more complex. Airtable, whimsical, Canva, InVideo. They're very robust products. And so it's very easy to get lost in their editors. I think what all of those companies are trying to do for their respective verticals and use cases is they're trying to democratize access to fades that previously you have to rely on professionals for. Maybe in the case of bayer team bot, it's your engineers. In the case of PM bot, it is professional graphic designers. In the case of a video, it's professional video editors. So when they're trying to democratize access, but they're also trying to make the products robust enough to be comparable to a professional great quality. And it's a very difficult place to play it, right? It's like, how do you make it simple enough where a nonprofessional can use it, but robust enough where they go and say, "Oh yeah, this is as good as if I would've hired a professional fill in the blank."
turns.zh: 几乎总是。我的很多工作就在那种专业消费者空间。所以产品往往更复杂。Airtable、Whimsical、Canva、InVideo。它们都是很强大的产品。所以很容易在它们的编辑器里迷路。我觉得所有这些公司，在各自垂直领域和用例里想做的，是把以前必须依赖专业人士的能力民主化。比如在 Airtable 那里，是你的工程师。在 Canva 那里，是专业平面设计师。在视频那里，是专业视频剪辑。所以他们想民主化这种能力，又想让产品足够强大、能跟专业级品质媲美。这是个很难玩的位置，对吧？怎么做到既简单到非专业人士能用，又强大到让他们说：“哦对，这跟请个专业 [填空] 一样好。”

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: And that's where onboarding, sorry for the long answer. That's where onboarding is really, really important because there's such a huge difference between landing someone on that initial editor page, be it Airtable, Canva having that left to their own devices versus getting as much information or as much relevant information front and then customizing that landing experience for them. So that if they're there to do X and we know XYZ about them, we're able to guide them and not expose them to the robustness of the product all at once. So the short answer is almost all the time onboarding is a big opportunity.
turns.zh: 而那就是上手流程——抱歉回答太长——那就是上手流程真正、真正重要的地方，因为在“让人落到初始编辑器页面（不管是 Airtable 还是 Canva）、然后任其自生自灭”和“把尽可能多、尽可能相关的信息前置、并为他们定制那个落地体验”之间，差别巨大。所以如果他们来是为了做 X，而我们知道关于他们的 XYZ，我们就能引导他们，而不是一下子把产品的全部复杂度都暴露给他们。所以简短的答案是：几乎任何时候，上手流程都是个大机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's what I was expecting to hear, to give folks some context. What's kind of an order magnitude that you've seen improvement on onboarding and maybe impact on a company improving onboarding.
turns.zh: 太好了。这正是我期待听到的。给大家点背景。你观察到的上手流程改进，大概是什么数量级的提升，也许对公司的影响？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Earlier stage companies where still haven't really approached the local maximal, but you haven't experimented with a ton of things. I mean, you can two to four X activation rates easily through onboarding. I think later stage companies like maybe Series B beyond, I think you can still probably get to 20 to 30% lift at activations. It depends on how many low hanging fruit are left to tackle.
turns.zh: 更早阶段的公司，还没真正接近局部最优、也还没试过一大堆东西的，我意思是，你很容易通过上手流程把激活率翻 2 到 4 倍。我觉得后期公司，比如 B 轮往后，大概还能拿到 20% 到 30% 的激活提升。取决于还剩多少低垂的果实可摘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. Yeah. Till the onboarding, there's always money in the onboarding banana stand. On that kind of same idea, do you have a general feeling of investments in this stuff often pays off and helps you grow and is often higher ROI and investments in bucket B are rarely successful. What would those two buckets be?
turns.zh: 有道理。对，上手流程里永远有钱——“上手流程香蕉摊里永远有钱”。顺着同一个思路，你总体感觉是：投这类东西经常有回报、帮你增长、而且往往 ROI 比投 B 类更高，而投 B 类很少成功？那两类分别是什么？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: So thinking of investments rawly, right? Not just monetarily.
turns.zh: 所以说到投入，是广义的，对吧？不只是钱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Time and resources.
turns.zh: 对，对。时间和资源。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I would say that getting to know your customer always pays off. So it's user interviews and getting to know your market, your customers, and your prospects always pays off. Customer research, inside surveying, interviewing panels incredibly useful. And I found that to be very especially early stages. The amount of clarity at momentum that it can create inside of a seed Series A up to Series B company when you first do some proper research push. The way it can galvanize the team and give them focus and clarity and purpose is remarkable. So that always pays off. What doesn't pay off? I mean, I think over reliance on paid, it comes to bite you in the rear end. When I think about tracking an attribution, I think it's a question of the right level of investment at the right stage.
turns.zh: 对。我会说，了解你的客户永远有回报。所以用户访谈、了解你的市场、客户和潜在客户，永远有回报。客户研究、内部调研、访谈小组，极其有用。我发现早期阶段尤其如此。当你第一次认真做一轮研究推送时，它给一家种子轮到 A 轮、乃至 B 轮的公司内部带来的清晰度和势头（momentum），是惊人的。它能如何团结团队、给他们聚焦、清晰和目标感，很了不起。所以这永远有回报。什么没有回报？我觉得过度依赖付费，迟早会咬你屁股。说到追踪和归因，我觉得是“在对的阶段做对的投入水平”的问题。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Rarely do companies get it right. They usually fall into one of two buckets where they underinvest in attribution and they are now, their budgets are up high. They have a broad channel portfolio and they have a hard time figuring out what's working, what isn't and they just get into this inertia. It's like, "Well, overall, the company's been growing and it's been growing roughly over the same time that we've been increasing our spend. We're scared to break it. So we're just going to keep spending." Or companies that read horror stories about other companies overspending. They sometimes try to invest in attribution too much, believe it or not where they're trying to get everything perfect and scientifically pure. But what they don't realize is that the payoff may not always be there. And so how do I fit this into your question of, I think tracking attribution incrementality is definitely a worthwhile investment arena, but it could both be a good or bad depending on the level. So you got to make sure the level investment is appropriate for your stage when you stand to aim for-
turns.zh: 公司很少做对。他们通常掉进两类之一：一类是归因投入不足，现在预算上去了、渠道组合铺开了，却很难搞清楚什么管用什么不进，于是陷入惯性：“嗯，整体公司在增长，而且大概跟我们加大投入同时发生。我们不敢动它。所以就继续烧。”另一类是读了别的公司过度烧钱的血泪故事，有时候反而试图在归因上投入过度——信不信由你——想让一切完美、科学纯净。但他们没意识到，回报未必总在那儿。所以怎么把它装回你的问题里：我觉得追踪归因和增量性绝对是个值得投的领域，但它是好是坏，取决于投入的水平。所以你得确保投入水平适合你的阶段，当你瞄准——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. You're such a good interviewee that you come back to the question.
turns.zh: 太好了。你真是个好受访者，会回到问题本身。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: No, that I promise.
turns.zh: 不，我保证。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was great. Okay. One last question. Before we get to our very exciting lightning round. I'd love you to get your thoughts on advertising on TikTok and YouTube and broadly is there any other tactics, avenues that you think are kind of underutilized or emerging that folks should be thinking about?
turns.zh: 那很好。好。最后一个问题。在我们进入超刺激的快问快答之前。我想听听你对在 TikTok 和 YouTube 上打广告的想法，广义地说，还有没有其他你觉得被低估或正在兴起、大家该想想的战术或渠道？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah. So TikTok, one thing I'll say about TikTok is I'm seeing it come up more and more as a channel that works well. And sometimes even the most efficient channel, most efficient digital channel for some brands. But I think that the thing about TikTok that oftentimes I was surprised about is you often hear, "Oh, TikTok that's for the 15 to 22 year olds." I'm bad with my gens Z and oh, my audience is different. So I'm just going to ignore the champ. TikTok has so many users and it's still so relatively unsaturated with advertisers that your audience is on there. You'd be surprised.
turns.zh: 好。TikTok，关于它我想说一点：我看到它作为一个管用的渠道出现得越来越多，有时候甚至是某些品牌最高效的渠道、最高效的数字渠道。但我经常对 TikTok 感到意外的一点是，你常听人说：“哦，TikTok 是给 15 到 22 岁的人用的。”我对 Z 世代的代际分不清，哦，我的受众不一样。所以我就忽略这个渠道。TikTok 有这么多用户，而且相对广告主来说还那么不饱和，你的受众就在上面。你会惊讶的。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I've worked with brands that their core demo is like 40 plus married making 200K plus in household annual income. And you wouldn't think that demo is on TikTok and it is. So what point about TikTok? Other channels, I think out at home is still not getting enough love. Podcasts? Okay. Yep, yep.
turns.zh: 我合作过的品牌，核心人群是 40 岁以上、已婚、家庭年收入 20 万美元以上。你不会觉得那群人在 TikTok 上，但他们就在。所以关于 TikTok 这点？其他渠道，我觉得直邮（direct mail）还没得到足够的爱。播客？对。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Spots through this one. I recall you heard it from Yuriy.
turns.zh: 通过这期播客听到了。你从 Yuriy 这儿听到的。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Direct mail, what has happened? They've gotten better with attribution because before a lot of those channels were written off as sort of attribution is just too hard on there and attribution is so good and reliable on digital. So that's that gap that canyon that existed in attribution capabilities of online and offline, deterred a lot of people from offline. Today offline has gotten better and actually positioning themselves as being able to do attribution, but also online attribution is deteriorated. So all of a sudden that argument kind of slimmed out a little bit and I'm seeing offline get a lot more traction and in podcasts, especially are actually very, very performant for a lot of brands. Those are a couple of things that come to mind.
turns.zh: 直邮，怎么了？它的归因变好了，因为以前很多这类渠道被直接划掉，理由是“归因太难”，而数字的归因又那么好、那么可靠。所以线上线下归因能力的这道鸿沟、这个大峡谷，劝退了很多人做线下。今天线下变好了，而且真的把自己定位成能做归因，而线上归因在退化。所以突然之间那个论点有点被削平了，我看到线下、尤其是播客，对很多品牌其实非常有转化力。这几样是我能想到的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Those are great. Happy to hear the podcast piece. Excellent. And then I actually, I'm an investor in a startup that Databig at a home campaign and they just told me that it was a 10 to one positive ROI on the deals that they got out of it. So I've been seeing that too, and that's such a good point that the measurement and attribution online has come down where it maybe makes more sense to try stuff like that. Amazing. All right. Are you ready for our very exciting lightning round? I'm going to ask you five questions I think, and then just, yeah, let's go through it quick.
turns.zh: 那些都很好。很高兴听到播客这块。太好了。而且我其实是一家做家庭活动（at-home campaign）的创业公司的投资人，他们刚告诉我，从那拿到的交易有 10 比 1 的正 ROI。所以我也观察到了，而且你这点说得太好了——线上的衡量和归因在下降，也许反而更值得去试这种东西。太棒了。好。准备好我们超刺激的快问快答了吗？我想问你五个问题，然后我们就快速过一遍。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 来吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. Okay. What are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 来吧。好。你最推荐给别人的一两本或两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Ooh, that's something that I think is very wrong to recency bias, right? It's like, what are some of the books you've read recently that you've enjoyed? But I would say there are a couple of books that stuck with me over the years. I think on the business side, where on the business side productivity side, it's a book called Essentialism. I forget the author's name. I think his last name is McKeown or something. And it's basically the book about cutting out the noise and finding a singular focus and doing that really well. It's a book that was a game changer for me at Grammarly being sort of new in my career, having really aggressive goals, not being scared to say no. Taking on a lot, just feel it thinking like, "Well, I'm only working 12 hours a day. There's 12 more left. I can do it."
turns.zh: 哦，这个我觉得很容易有近因偏差，对吧？就是“你最近读了什么喜欢的书？”但我会说有几本这些年一直留在我心里的书。商业侧、效率侧，有一本叫《本质主义》（Essentialism）。我忘了作者名，好像姓 McKeown 之类的。它基本是讲砍掉噪音、找到单一聚焦并把那件事做好的书。这本书在 Grammarly 对我是个 game changer，当时我职业生涯还新，目标很激进，不怕说不。接很多活，就觉得：“我才干 12 小时，还有 12 小时，我能行。”

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: And then when you end up stepping into a leadership role, which happened for me, I mean, that happened prior to grounded, but really I was able to grow into that role at Grammarly. That book was incredible and I used it a lot. I pretty much got copies for everybody on the team, like 40 plus people. So that is a book I swear by.
turns.zh: 然后当你踏入领导角色——这发生在我身上，其实在 Grammarly 之前就开始了，但我是在 Grammarly 真正长进那个角色的——那本书太棒了，我用很多。我基本给团队所有人，40 多号人，都发了 copy。所以这是我誓死信赖的一本书。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I read a lot outside of work and business. So I don't know if it's appropriate, but I'll say that. It's Frankl's, A Man's Search for Meaning is just a remarkable memoir on perseverance and I think that biggest takeaway is you can't control what's happening around you, but you can control your reaction to it. And then I'd say the book that I read recently, because I was very affected by the Russia invasion of Ukraine. I'm originally from Ukraine. I believe you are as well. So it hit very close to home and there have been a lot of references drawn between the President's Zelensky and his response in the war and Winston Churchill's response in 1941 when Hitler started marching through Europe. And so I read a book called I think The Splendid and the Vile by Eric Larson.
turns.zh: 我在工作、商业之外读很多。所以我不知道合不合适，但我说一个。弗兰克尔的《活出意义来》（A Man's Search for Meaning）就是一本关于韧性的非凡回忆录，我觉得最大的收获是：你控制不了周围发生的事，但你能控制你对它的反应。然后我会说最近读的一本，因为乌克兰被入侵对我打击很大。我来自乌克兰。我相信你也是。所以这事离我很近，而且大家经常把泽连斯基总统在战争中的反应，和丘吉尔 1941 年希特勒横扫欧洲时的反应相提并论。所以我读了一本叫《光辉与阴暗》（The Splendid and the Vile），作者 Eric Larson。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I read that. I read that.
turns.zh: 对。我读过。我读过。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Did you also read it since the invasion?
turns.zh: 你也是入侵之后读的吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, it was before that, but I totally get that now.
turns.zh: 不，在那之前，但我现在完全懂了。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Reading it right now because I've been following the conflict very closely, but for people who haven't followed the conflict or maybe have only followed the rush, the war kind of in a cursory way, you can put what's happening into historical context remarkably well. So I feel like that book accomplishes two things. Number one, it's like you learned something about not so distant history that maybe you didn't know, which was about Great Britain and Winston Churchill kind of courageous response in the face of Hitler's invasion of Europe. But you also can draw so many parallels to what's happening today. And hopefully that helps us understand what's at stake, not to end on two grandiose of a note.
turns.zh: 我现在正在读，因为我一直紧紧关注这场冲突，但对没关注或只是粗略关注的人来说，你能把正在发生的事放进历史语境里，做得好得惊人。所以我觉得那本书完成了两件事。第一，你学到了一些也许不知道的、不那么久远的历史——关于英国和丘吉尔面对希特勒入侵欧洲时的勇敢反应。但你也能从中拉出那么多跟今天类比（parallels）的地方。希望这帮我们理解利害所在，别收在太宏大的调子上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We'll go less grandiose quickly, but I will add one thing that stood out in that book that is also true in the Ukraine is how during the fire bombing of Britain, people are just going out every day, going to clubs, still having-
turns.zh: 我们很快就会不那么宏大，但我要加一点那本书里让我印象深刻、在乌克兰也一样真实的事：在英国遭受燃烧弹轰炸期间，人们每天照常出门、去俱乐部、依然在——

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: I know. Steal them their life.
turns.zh: 我知道。偷回他们的生活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And same thing even today in Ukraine is.
turns.zh: 今天乌克兰也一样。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: And not just keep, but it's very life.
turns.zh: 而且不只是坚持，是好好地生活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Okay. We'll move on to less, less serious stuff maybe. What a transition to, what's your favorite other podcast?
turns.zh: 我喜欢。好。我们转到没那么宏大、也许轻松点的东西。你最喜欢的其他播客是什么？

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Honestly, there's only one other podcast that I'll listen to right now because I've just been so consumed. I listened to a lot of live streams and read a lot about the conflict, which has taken up so much of my head space. That's not work related, but I would say that the All in Pod. I feel like it's a cool way for me to just catch up on everything that's going on through their unique filter.
turns.zh: 说实话，我现在只听另一个播客，因为我太沉浸了。我听很多直播、读很多关于冲突的东西，占了太多脑子。这不是工作相关的，但我会说 All-In 播客（All in Pod）。我觉得它是我用一种很酷的方式，通过他们独特的滤镜追上所有正在发生的事的途径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: That's probably the-
turns.zh: 那大概是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Yeah. I learned a lot.
turns.zh: 酷。对。我学到很多。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: I learned a lot from that one. That's so much drama on that show. Okay. Great. Favorite recent movie or TV show. Anything stand out.
turns.zh: 我从那档学到很多。那节目戏剧性太强了。好。好。最近喜欢的电影或剧。有什么出挑的？

turns.en: So that's another thing. Since February I've watched nothing. My Netflix skew just keeps growing because they keep emailing me saying this new season is out. I'm like, "Oh yeah. I used to that show. Let me add it to the queue." I mean, recently I had some downtime. The kids were with grandma, so I watch movie Hustle with Adam Sandler.
turns.zh: 这又是另一件事。从二月起我什么都没看。我的 Netflix 队列一直在涨，因为他们一直邮件跟我说新一季出了。我就：“哦对，我以前看那剧。加进队列吧。”最近有点 downtime。孩子们跟奶奶去了，所以我看了 Adam Sandler 演的《必胜球探》（Hustle）。

turns.en: Love that. So good.
turns.zh: 爱那部。太好了。

turns.en: Yeah. It was good. It was it's very light. It's not like a movie that's going to make you think a lot, but it was just good old entertainment. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。不错。很轻松。不是那种让你想很多的电影，但就是老派的好娱乐。对。

turns.en: I like that. I like that summary. Yeah, it was so delightful. Maybe one more question. Who else in the industry do you most respect as a thought leader? Maybe someone people may not know or if anyone else comes to mind.
turns.zh: 我喜欢。我喜欢那个总结。对，太让人愉悦了。也许再一个问题。行业里你最尊重哪位思想领袖？也许是大家可能不认识的，或者任何想到的。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: That's a very good question. So I would say first off, I do believe that some of the brightest minds, honestly, in any craft are people that you never hear because it takes a certain personality, energy, and probably a lot of other circumstances to invest in your personal brand. And also it's very hard to do that while still staying relevant as a practitioner. I mean, when I think about myself two years ago before starting advising, I was just kind of living in my Grammarly cave. And I felt like I was probably at the top of my craft, but I didn't have time to pick my head up or not, maybe not even just tie, but I didn't know where to start to pick my head up and do something like this. I would say some people that, I mean, I mentioned Ethan in terms of SEO. SEO and just organic growth loops and content as a growth engine, he is best in class.
turns.zh: 好问题。首先我会说，我确实相信，在任何手艺里，一些最聪明的大脑是你从没听过的，因为要经营个人品牌，需要某种性格、精力，可能还有很多其他条件。而且在做从业者（practitioner）的同时还保持不被淘汰（relevant），也很难。说到两年前的我，在开始做顾问之前，我就是窝在我的 Grammarly 洞穴里。我觉得自己大概处在手艺的顶端，但我没时间抬头——也许不只是没时间，是我不知道从哪开始抬头、做这种事。我会说一些人，我提过 Ethan，在 SEO 方面。SEO 以及有机增长闭环、把内容当增长引擎，他是顶级水准。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Who else? So Mark Fisk, he shows up in the Reforge chats a lot. He was leading growth and marketing at Credit Karma for a while. And right now he's an investor I think at the HRG Capital, but he is a really, really strong thought leader on all things, performance marketing attribution, and just kind of paid acquisition at large. Those are two people that I make sure I... And there are others of course, but those are two who I make sure I stay in touch with at least on a quarterly basis because any casual catch up just yield so many unique nuggets.
turns.zh: 还有谁？Mark Fisk，他经常出现在 Reforge 的讨论里。他曾在 Credit Karma 管增长和营销一阵子。现在他好像是 HRG Capital 的投资人，但他在效果营销、归因、广义付费获客方面，是个非常强的思想领袖。这两个人我会确保我……当然还有别人，但这两个我确保至少每季度保持联系，因为任何一次随意的 catch up 都能产出那么多独特的金句。

turns.en: Amazing. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, learn more and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。大家想联系你、了解更多，能在哪找到你？听众能怎么帮到你？

turns.en: Honestly, I don't have a very strong online presence. I would say LinkedIn is probably the only place where I seek things the recent, so folks can find me there. They can also find me inside of Lenny's Newsletter. I do. I do. I do, but you can appearance there once in a while and on that's odd.
turns.zh: 说实话，我线上存在感不强。我会说 LinkedIn 大概是唯一我发点近况的地方，所以大家能在那找到我。他们也能在 Lenny 的通讯（Newsletter）里找到我。我确实会在那偶尔露个面，虽然那有点怪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: True.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: How folks can be helpful to me, honestly, promote and shout out of Lenny's Newsletter and Lenny's Pod and that if you're building awesome things, come talk to me. So it's about it.
turns.zh: 大家怎么帮我，说实话，宣传、为大喊 Lenny 的通讯和 Lenny 的播客，还有如果你在做很棒的东西，来找我聊。我总会在生活里拨出一些时间，纯粹做非商业的事，就是跟创始人聊、在电话上花 30 分钟，不图任何回报，也许能帮他们省点时间、别犯我犯过的错，帮他们指一条更顺的路。就这些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. You are awesome. Thank you so much for making the time to do this. I learned a ton. I can't wait to get this episode out. There's just so much meat to this thing,
turns.zh: 太棒了。你太厉害了。非常感谢你抽时间来做这期。我学到太多了。我等不及要把这期发出来了。这期干货太多了——

turns.speaker: Yuriy Timen
turns.en: Dude this was good.
turns.zh: 哥们儿这期真好。

turns.en: I feel like my nervousness was unfounded. This was super organic. You are just as welcoming as you are outside of the pod. So yeah. Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 我觉得我之前的紧张是没必要的。这期太自然了。你跟播客外一样让人如沐春风。所以，谢谢邀请我。
